analysis.one_liner: Imposes testing, paid sick leave, reporting, and strike-team rules on nursing homes during COVID-19.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced May 7, 2020 with 3 Senate sponsors, was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and never received a hearing, vote, or floor action before Congress ended January 3, 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have added pandemic-era requirements for nursing homes that serve Medicare and Medicaid patients: weekly testing of residents, testing of staff before every shift, two weeks of paid sick leave for every employee, daily public reporting of cases, deaths, and protective equipment supplies, and $10,000-per-day fines for violations. It would also fund state 'strike teams' to respond within 72 hours when outbreaks hit, and require the government to end certain waivers of nursing home rules once facilities could comply. It sat in committee and died.
analysis.who_benefits: Nursing home residents and their families, and the aides and nurses who work in these facilities. Residents would get weekly testing, protection from being discharged to make room for COVID-19 patients, guaranteed return within 180 days if they left to stay with family, and public, daily data on outbreaks. Workers would get pre-shift testing, education on transmission, protective equipment shortage reporting, and two weeks of paid sick leave, so they would not have to work while sick.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Nursing home residents and their aides

how_it_helps.text: Requires skilled nursing and Medicaid nursing facilities to test residents weekly and staff before each shift, or screen for symptoms and report daily if testing kits are short [S3].
Requires facilities to provide at least two weeks of paid sick leave to each employee during the emergency, 'notwithstanding any other provision of law' [S3].

Requires daily reporting of cases, deaths (with age and race/ethnicity), protective equipment supplies, and staffing levels, with publication within 24 hours on the Nursing Home Compare and COVIDView websites [S3].

Bars facilities from discharging or transferring residents to free up beds for COVID-19 patients without state survey agency approval, written notice 72 hours in advance, and the resident's written consent, and guarantees a resident who moved out to stay with family a right to return within 180 days after the emergency ends [S3].

Authorizes $500 million for state strike teams that would deploy within 72 hours to any facility with three or more residents or staff diagnosed or suspected of COVID-19, to separate the exposed, supervise testing, and enforce whistleblower protections [S3].
Imposes a $10,000-per-day civil penalty on facility operators for each day of violation of the care, safety, or reporting requirements, or for reporting false information [S3].
Requires facilities to notify all residents, their representatives, and employees within 12 hours of a COVID-19 diagnosis or death, and to post notices at entrances while infections are present [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Nursing home operators, including the large for-profit chains that dominate the sector, would bear the cost of testing, paid sick leave, an infection preventionist on staff, daily reporting, and potential fines of $10,000 per violation per day. Taxpayers would fund the $500 million strike-team program. Facilities with insufficient test kits would have to report the shortfall daily rather than being excused from testing.

drawbacks.text: The bill imposed most requirements as unfunded mandates: facilities received no direct money for weekly resident testing, pre-shift staff testing, or two weeks of paid sick leave, and many operators were already financially strained during the pandemic [S3].

Facilities that lacked testing kits were not excused; they had to screen for symptoms and report the shortfall daily, so a chronic national kit shortage would have created a steady stream of noncompliance reports without itself solving supply [S3].

The $10,000-per-day penalty applied to each day of any violation of the sweeping care, safety, and reporting requirements, raising the risk that facilities would face steep fines over paperwork and supply shortfalls rather than unsafe care [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The stakes were high: nursing homes accounted for a large share of COVID-19 deaths in 2020, and the bill targeted the exact failures that drove them — untested staff, understaffing, hidden case counts, and residents' protections being waived. The main costs fell on operators, whose facilities are largely paid with public Medicare and Medicaid money, and the bill's testing requirements depended on supplies the federal government had not secured. A fair-minded reader could object to the unfunded mandates and the blunt penalty structure, but the bill died without any hearing or negotiation where those issues could have been addressed.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced and stayed there through the end of the Congress in January 2021, with no hearing, markup, or vote.

narrative.text: Sen. Booker introduced the bill on May 7, 2020, with Sen. Blumenthal as an original cosponsor, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance the same day [S3][S5].
Two Senate Democrats are listed as cosponsors, both from the same party as the sponsor [S4].
The action history shows only introduction and committee referral; no committee action, no report, no floor vote, and no further action through the end of the 116th Congress [S5].
The CRS summary confirms the bill's requirements — testing, paid sick leave, daily reporting, and strike teams — remained as introduced, with no amended version produced [S2].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nursing home operators, who avoided the testing, sick leave, reporting, and $10,000-per-day fine requirements for the duration of the pandemic.

industries.industry: Nursing home operators (skilled nursing and Medicaid nursing facilities)
industries.note: The bill would have required operators to pay for weekly resident testing, pre-shift staff testing, two weeks of paid sick leave, a full-time infection preventionist, and daily reporting, and exposed them to $10,000-per-day fines. Operators continued collecting Medicare and Medicaid payments while avoiding these new costs because the bill never advanced.
The weekly testing mandates would have created large, sustained demand for testing kits. The bill also required facilities to report kit shortages daily rather than accept screening as a substitute.
